title: Innate Immunity Barriers & Cytokine Signaling
quickSummary: Innate immunity: non-specific, present at birth. 4 defense barriers: Physical (Skin, Mucus), Physiological (Stomach HCl, Lysozyme in tears/saliva), Cellular (PMN-Neutrophils, Monocytes, Macrophages, Natural Killer NK cells), and Cytokine barriers (Interferons IFN-alpha, beta, gamma produced by virus-infected cells to protect healthy neighbors).

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Innate immunity comprises non-specific defenses present from birth across 4 barrier systems: (1) Physical (skin keratin and mucosal lining); (2) Physiological (gastric HCl and lysozyme); (3) Cellular (phagocytic PMN-neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and cytotoxic NK cells); (4) Cytokine barriers (antiviral Interferons).

conceptBreakdown.content:
### 3.1 Four Defense Barriers of Innate Immunity
1. **Physical Barriers**:
   - **Skin**: Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium acts as an impermeable mechanical barrier preventing entry of micro-organisms.
   - **Mucus Coating**: Epithelial lining of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts traps inhaled and ingested pathogens for ciliary clearance.
2. **Physiological Barriers**:
   - **Gastric Acid ($\text{HCl}$)**: Low $\text{pH } 1.5\text{--}2.0$ kills ingested bacteria in the stomach.
   - **Lysozyme**: Enzymatic agent present in tears, saliva, and sweat that hydrolyzes $\beta(1\rightarrow 4)$ glycosidic bonds in bacterial peptidoglycan cell walls.
3. **Cellular Barriers**:
   - **Polymorphonuclear Leukocytes (PMN-Neutrophils)** and **Monocytes**: Phagocytose and destroy invading bacteria in bloodstream.
   - **Tissue Macrophages** (e.g., Kupffer cells in liver, Alveolar macrophages in lungs, Microglia in brain).
   - **Natural Killer (NK) Cells**: Large granular lymphocytes that recognize and lyse virus-infected cells and tumor cells without prior sensitization via perforin and granzymes.
4. **Cytokine Barriers & Interferon Signaling**:
   - Virus-infected cells produce and secrete antiviral glycoproteins called **Interferons ($\text{IFN}-\alpha, \text{IFN}-\beta, \text{IFN}-\gamma$).**
   - **Mechanism**: Interferons diffuse to uninfected neighboring cells and bind cell-surface receptors, inducing the transcription of **Antiviral Proteins (AVPs)** (such as $2',5'$-oligoadenylate synthetase and Protein Kinase R), which degrade viral mRNA and halt protein translation upon viral invasion.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs)
conceptBreakdown.title: Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs)
conceptBreakdown.content: Innate immune cells recognize Pathogen-Associated Molecular Patterns (PAMPs, like bacterial LPS or viral dsRNA) using Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs) such as Toll-Like Receptors (TLR4, TLR3).

conceptBreakdown.heading: Inflammatory Response & Histamine
conceptBreakdown.title: Inflammatory Response & Histamine
conceptBreakdown.content: Tissue damage triggers mast cells to release histamine and prostaglandins, causing local vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and neutrophil extravasation (diapedesis).
